The question is what must be shared, and when

Distributed LLM execution partitions work and state across devices. The goal is to fit the workload, increase useful throughput, or reduce latency. Every partition introduces a dependency: a partial result, a parameter shard, a gradient, an expert token, or a cached prefix must reach its consumer.

This guide connects mathematical collectives, training parallelism, long-context attention, distributed serving, and low-communication training. It uses primary papers and current project documentation checked through 25 September 2026. Read the MoE and KV guides for deeper treatment of expert routing and cache storage.

The core problem: place ownership and schedule dependencies

A distributed algorithm is a statement about who owns each tensor, which values are replicated, when a consumer can proceed, and which numerical semantics survive the partition. The communication primitives are consequences of those choices. Naming TP, PP and DP degrees without the ownership map leaves the important part unspecified.

The objective differs between training and serving. Training generally minimizes time or cost to a target quality, subject to memory capacity and optimizer semantics. Serving generally maximizes useful completed requests under TTFT and token-latency constraints, subject to state residency and quality. A faster training step that uses a statistically inefficient global batch can lose overall; a higher serving throughput that violates a user's deadline is not a successful optimization.

G=(V,E),V={compute, transfer, synchronization, allocation}E={data dependencies, resource ordering}Titeration≥max⁡π∈paths(G)∑v∈πtvTiteration≥max⁡rWrβr,effectiveMpeak=max⁡t∑a∈live(t)Ma\begin{aligned}G&=(V,E),\quad V=\{\text{compute, transfer, synchronization, allocation}\}\\ E&=\{\text{data dependencies, resource ordering}\}\\ T_{\mathrm{iteration}}&\ge\max_{\pi\in\mathrm{paths}(G)}\sum_{v\in\pi}t_v\\ T_{\mathrm{iteration}}&\ge\max_r\frac{W_r}{\beta_{r,\mathrm{effective}}}\\ M_{\mathrm{peak}}&=\max_t\sum_{a\in\mathrm{live}(t)}M_a\end{aligned}GETiteration​Titeration​Mpeak​​=(V,E),V={compute, transfer, synchronization, allocation}={data dependencies, resource ordering}≥π∈paths(G)max​v∈π∑​tv​≥rmax​βr,effective​Wr​​=tmax​a∈live(t)∑​Ma​​

The two time bounds explain why “communication volume” is incomplete. A large gradient reduction can be hidden under backward work; a tiny tensor-parallel reduction may block every next layer. The memory bound explains why summing steady-state parameter shards is incomplete: gathered weights, saved activations, prefetch buffers and in-flight sends can peak together.

These are overlapping branches. FSDP did not replace TP, and disaggregation did not make chunked prefill irrelevant. A real system composes them where their costs fit. The chapters follow these dependency changes, with original schedule/layout figures and explicit derivations.

Communication primitives and the α–β model

A rank is a process participating in a communication group. A collective defines a group operation; the library chooses an implementation based on topology, message size, and available transport. NCCL terminology is useful even when working with another vendor’s library. [1]

OperationInput and outputTypical LLM use
All-reduceEvery rank contributes a tensor; every rank gets the reductionReplicated data-parallel gradients; TP partial outputs
Reduce-scatterReduce tensors, then give each rank one result shardSharded gradient ownership; sequence-parallel output
All-gatherGather each rank’s shard onto every rankMaterialize sharded parameters or activations
All-to-allEach rank sends a different partition to each peerExpert routing; Ulysses sequence/head transpose
BroadcastOne source distributes identical dataInitialization and synchronization
Point-to-pointOne sender transfers to one receiverPipeline activation or KV migration
Tmessage≈α+mβα=startup latency,m=bytes,β=effective bytes/sTring≈2(p−1)α+2(p−1)mpβVsent/rank≈2(p−1)mp\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{message}}&\approx\alpha+\frac m\beta\\ \alpha&=\text{startup latency},\quad m=\text{bytes},\quad\beta=\text{effective bytes/s}\\ T_{\mathrm{ring}}&\approx2(p-1)\alpha+\frac{2(p-1)m}{p\beta}\\ V_{\mathrm{sent/rank}}&\approx\frac{2(p-1)m}{p}\end{aligned}Tmessage​αTring​Vsent/rank​​≈α+βm​=startup latency,m=bytes,β=effective bytes/s≈2(p−1)α+pβ2(p−1)m​≈p2(p−1)m​​

A ring uses bandwidth well for large tensors but pays many startup steps. Tree algorithms can reduce latency for small messages; hierarchical algorithms exploit fast links within a node and slower links between nodes. These are models, not a guarantee that the runtime will choose a particular schedule.

Idealized ring cost; MB and GB are decimal. Link contention, topology, protocol thresholds, and reduction compute are omitted.

At p=8, m=256 MB, β=50 GB/s, and α=5 μs, the model predicts roughly 9.03 ms. For a 1 MB message it predicts about 0.105 ms, with much more relative startup cost. Combining tiny gradient buckets reduces launches, but waiting for a larger bucket can delay overlap with backward computation.

Units matter: a 400 Gb/s network interface is 50 GB/s before overhead. A quoted bidirectional link rate cannot be treated as one-way effective bandwidth. GPU-to-NIC placement, PCIe paths, switch oversubscription, and competing traffic all affect β.

Collectives in depth: algorithm, topology and critical path

Derive the ring rather than memorize the formula

Split each rank's m-byte tensor into p chunks. In reduce-scatter, every rank sends one chunk to its neighbor, receives another chunk, reduces it with its own contribution and forwards the partial reduction. After p−1 steps, each rank owns one fully reduced chunk. All-gather then circulates those finished chunks for another p−1 steps. Each stage moves m/p bytes per rank, giving the familiar 2(p−1)m/p payload and 2(p−1) startups.

This algorithm avoids a central server and balances traffic on a suitable ring. But a logical ring can map poorly to physical links: one slow cross-node edge or shared PCIe path can throttle progress. Multiple rings/channels can exploit independent paths, at the cost of more concurrent traffic and kernel resources. Effective bandwidth in the formula must already account for that placement and contention.

A recursive-doubling all-reduce exchanges progressively combined values with partners at distances 1,2,4,… for log2(p) stages when p is a power of two. It pays fewer startups but can move a full tensor at each stage in its simple form. A reduce-scatter/all-gather algorithm based on recursive halving/doubling combines logarithmic startup stages with bandwidth-efficient payload, but message sizes and topology interactions differ. “Tree is for small messages; ring is for large messages” is a useful intuition, not a universal implementation rule.

Tring≈2(p−1)α+2(p−1)mpβTdoubling≈log⁡2(p)α+log⁡2(p)mβThalving+doubling≈2log⁡2(p)α+2(p−1)mpβHomogeneous model; p is a power of two.Reduction, protocol, topology and concurrent traffic omitted.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{ring}}&\approx2(p-1)\alpha+\frac{2(p-1)m}{p\beta}\\ T_{\mathrm{doubling}}&\approx\log_2(p)\alpha+\frac{\log_2(p)m}{\beta}\\ T_{\mathrm{halving+doubling}}&\approx2\log_2(p)\alpha+\frac{2(p-1)m}{p\beta}\\ &\text{Homogeneous model; }p\text{ is a power of two.}\\ &\text{Reduction, protocol, topology and concurrent traffic omitted.}\end{aligned}Tring​Tdoubling​Thalving+doubling​​≈2(p−1)α+pβ2(p−1)m​≈log2​(p)α+βlog2​(p)m​≈2log2​(p)α+pβ2(p−1)m​Homogeneous model; p is a power of two.Reduction, protocol, topology and concurrent traffic omitted.​

The last line does not imply every library should always choose recursive halving/doubling. A real network may have limited simultaneous injection, routing asymmetry or unfavorable partner placement. Chunking, pipelining, transport protocols and packet sizes determine whether the theoretical schedule keeps links busy. Benchmark the message-size distribution of the application, including small collectives on the critical path.

Hierarchical collectives separate expensive and cheap links

Suppose a node has eight accelerators with a fast internal fabric and one or more slower network interfaces. A hierarchical reduction first combines local contributions, performs an inter-node reduction on representative shards, then distributes results locally. The design should use all available NICs without transmitting redundant copies. If every tensor-parallel rank sends the same pipeline activation across nodes independently, local sharding followed by destination gathering can reduce duplicate network traffic. Megatron 3D explicitly studies such scatter/gather communication optimization. [3]

For all-to-all, endpoint bandwidth is only one bound. Let traffic matrix V[i,j] be bytes sent from rank i to rank j. Completion is constrained by the busiest sender, busiest receiver and busiest physical network cut. Uniform all-to-all microbenchmarks can therefore overestimate MoE performance when routing concentrates traffic on a small subset of experts or nodes.

Tall-to-all≥max⁡{max⁡i∑jVijβisend,  max⁡j∑iVijβjrecv,  max⁡cutVcrossingβcut}\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{all\text{-}to\text{-}all}}&\ge\max\left\{\max_i\frac{\sum_jV_{ij}}{\beta_i^{\mathrm{send}}},\;\max_j\frac{\sum_iV_{ij}}{\beta_j^{\mathrm{recv}}},\;\max_{\mathrm{cut}}\frac{V_{\mathrm{crossing}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{cut}}}\right\}\end{aligned}Tall-to-all​​≥max{imax​βisend​∑j​Vij​​,jmax​βjrecv​∑i​Vij​​,cutmax​βcut​Vcrossing​​}​

Derivation: hierarchical all-reduce and the shared-NIC trap

Topology and assumptions. There are n nodes with g ranks per node. Every rank contributes an m-byte tensor. Let αL,βL be local startup latency and effective bandwidth, and αN,βN the corresponding inter-node values per concurrent lane. Assume ideal ring stages, divisible tensors, and independent local/inter-node phases. Reduction arithmetic and network contention are omitted initially. The hierarchy below implements the same sum as an all-reduce; it changes data ownership while moving it. Collective semantics, Megatron 3D topology discussion.

1. Reduce-scatter locally. A g-rank ring has g−1 stages. Each stage sends m/g bytes, so each rank sends (g−1)m/g and finishes with one fully node-reduced shard of size m/g.

2. Reduce those shards across nodes. For every local shard index, its owners on the n nodes perform an all-reduce. There are g such lanes. Each lane communicates a tensor m/g bytes long, costing 2(n−1)αN+2(n−1)m/(ngβN) in the ring model.

3. All-gather locally. The g global result shards are distributed to every local rank. Adding the two local phases gives:

Thier≈2(g−1)αL+2(g−1)mgβL+2(n−1)αN+2(n−1)mngβN\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{hier}}&\approx2(g-1)\alpha_L+\frac{2(g-1)m}{g\beta_L}\\ &\quad+2(n-1)\alpha_N+\frac{2(n-1)m}{ng\beta_N}\end{aligned}Thier​​≈2(g−1)αL​+gβL​2(g−1)m​+2(n−1)αN​+ngβN​2(n−1)m​​

Why dividing the message by g is not a free g-fold speedup. If each lane has an independent NIC at bandwidth βN, the expression can exploit g NICs. If all lanes share one node injection budget Bnode, then βN≤Bnode/g under equal sharing. Substitution yields an inter-node bandwidth term at least 2(n−1)m/(nBnode): g cancels. The hierarchy still avoids redundant inter-node copies and can improve placement, but it cannot create network injection bandwidth.

Example. For n=8, g=8, m=1 GB and Bnode=100 GB/s, the inter-node bandwidth term is 2×7/(8×100)=17.5 ms. Treating all eight shards as if each independently received the full node NIC would predict 2.1875 ms and undercount by eight. All quantities here are decimal; startup and local movement still need to be added.

Exercise — When extra NICs actually help

Use the preceding n=g=8, m=1 GB system. Local startup is 2 μs, local bandwidth 400 GB/s, inter-node startup 5 μs. Compare a shared 100 GB/s node budget with eight independent 100 GB/s lanes. Compute the ideal full hierarchical times.

Show worked solution
Tlocal=2⋅7⋅2 μs+2⋅7⋅18⋅400 s=0.028+4.375=4.403 msTnetwork,startup=2⋅7⋅5 μs=0.070 msTshared,payload=17.5 msTindependent,payload=2⋅7⋅18⋅8⋅100 s=2.1875 msTshared≈21.973 ms,Tindependent≈6.6605 ms\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{local}}&=2\cdot7\cdot2\,\mu\mathrm{s}+\frac{2\cdot7\cdot1}{8\cdot400}\,\mathrm{s}\\ &=0.028+4.375=4.403\,\mathrm{ms}\\ T_{\mathrm{network,startup}}&=2\cdot7\cdot5\,\mu\mathrm{s}=0.070\,\mathrm{ms}\\ T_{\mathrm{shared,payload}}&=17.5\,\mathrm{ms}\\ T_{\mathrm{independent,payload}}&=\frac{2\cdot7\cdot1}{8\cdot8\cdot100}\,\mathrm{s}=2.1875\,\mathrm{ms}\\ T_{\mathrm{shared}}&\approx21.973\,\mathrm{ms},\quad T_{\mathrm{independent}}\approx6.6605\,\mathrm{ms}\end{aligned}Tlocal​Tnetwork,startup​Tshared,payload​Tindependent,payload​Tshared​​=2⋅7⋅2μs+8⋅4002⋅7⋅1​s=0.028+4.375=4.403ms=2⋅7⋅5μs=0.070ms=17.5ms=8⋅8⋅1002⋅7⋅1​s=2.1875ms≈21.973ms,Tindependent​≈6.6605ms​

The latter assumes eight usable independent lanes and sufficient fabric bisection capacity. A count of eight physical ports alone does not prove that the host, switch or routing policy can sustain that concurrency.

Overlap needs slack in both the dependency graph and hardware

Let C be compute time and N communication time for independent stages. Perfect overlap would replace C+N with max(C,N); exposed communication becomes max(0,N−C). This is a best case. If communication uses GPU SMs or HBM bandwidth required by the GEMM, both C and N may grow when run together. The right experiment compares the concurrent trace with the sum of isolated traces and records the resource contention.

Gradient buckets demonstrate the tradeoff. A small bucket becomes ready early and may overlap more of backward, but pays more launches/startups. A large bucket amortizes startup and improves bandwidth, but cannot begin until its last gradient is ready. Bucket boundaries should follow backward readiness and network scale, not just tensor size. Gradient accumulation can suppress synchronization on intermediate microbatches, but the implementation must preserve correct token/sample weighting.

Collective semantics also affect reproducibility. Floating-point addition is not associative, so a different reduction tree can change rounding even with the same real-number formula. Bitwise determinism, numerical equivalence and convergence equivalence are different claims. Dynamic control flow must still issue matching collectives in matching order on every participating rank; an otherwise valid local branch can deadlock a distributed program.

Stage 1: data parallelism and ZeRO

Replicated data parallel training

Each replica processes different data and synchronizes gradients before applying the same update. With correct loss normalization, this approximates a larger global batch under synchronous optimization. Gradient accumulation increases examples processed between synchronizations, but changes global batch or update frequency unless the configuration compensates.

Let P be parameters and d the data-parallel group size. A common mixed-precision Adam accounting uses 2 bytes for weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for master weights, and 8 for two FP32 moments. Actual implementations can store gradients or master weights differently.

Mreplicated=16PMZeRO-1=4P+12PdMZeRO-2=2P+14PdMZeRO-3=16Pd(persistent bytes/rank; gathered tensors excluded)\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{replicated}}&=16P\\M_{\mathrm{ZeRO\text{-}1}}&=4P+\frac{12P}{d}\\M_{\mathrm{ZeRO\text{-}2}}&=2P+\frac{14P}{d}\\M_{\mathrm{ZeRO\text{-}3}}&=\frac{16P}{d}\quad\text{(persistent bytes/rank; gathered tensors excluded)}\end{aligned}Mreplicated​MZeRO-1​MZeRO-2​MZeRO-3​​=16P=4P+d12P​=2P+d14P​=d16P​(persistent bytes/rank; gathered tensors excluded)​

ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state; ZeRO-2 also shards gradients; ZeRO-3 also shards parameters, materializing them when needed. The saved memory comes with scheduling and communication obligations. Fully sharded implementations follow this general pattern, but wrapping granularity and prefetch policies matter. Peak memory includes temporary all-gathers, activations, allocator overhead, and communication buffers. [7]

ZeRO-Infinity adds CPU/NVMe offload and coordinated prefetch to extend capacity beyond HBM. Capacity is useful only if transfers can be hidden or amortized. A configuration that fits but spends most time loading shards is a poor throughput configuration. [8]

Derivation: globally correct token gradients and clipping under sharding

Notation. Rank r sees nr valid target tokens after masking and has a local sum loss Sr=Σᵢℓr,i. The intended objective is one mean over all valid tokens, L=(Σr Sr)/(Σr nr), where token counts are independent of the current parameters for this batch. Some distributed runtimes average gradients across d ranks; others sum. This convention determines the local normalization. ZeRO changes ownership but should preserve the intended update.

1. Differentiate the intended objective.

N=∑rnr,∇L=1N∑r∇SrLr=dNSrif all-reduce averages1d∑r∇Lr=1N∑r∇Sr\begin{aligned}N&=\sum_r n_r,\qquad\nabla L=\frac1N\sum_r\nabla S_r\\ L_r&=\frac dN S_r\quad\text{if all-reduce averages}\\ \frac1d\sum_r\nabla L_r&=\frac1N\sum_r\nabla S_r\end{aligned}NLr​d1​r∑​∇Lr​​=r∑​nr​,∇L=N1​r∑​∇Sr​=Nd​Sr​if all-reduce averages=N1​r∑​∇Sr​​

If a rank first takes Sr/nr and then gradients are averaged, the result is (1/d)Σr∇Sr/nr. These are equal only when token counts match, or by a coincidental equality of gradients. Gradient accumulation introduces another index: sum the valid-token counts over all accumulated microbatches before choosing the normalization. Applying an extra division by the accumulation count after already dividing by the global token count would shrink the update again.

2. Derive clipping over unique gradient elements. Suppose the logical gradient vector is sharded into disjoint gr. Its norm obeys ||g||²=Σr||gr||². Reduce the local squared norms, take one square root, compute c=min(1,τ/||g||), and multiply every shard by the same c. If every rank instead holds a full replicated gradient, summing all d local norms counts each element d times and inflates the norm by √d. The reduction group must match ownership.

Example and interpretation. If one rank has 100 tokens with average scalar gradient 1 and another has 900 with average gradient 3, the correct result is (100+2700)/1000=2.8. Averaging rank means gives 2.0. Neither collective has malfunctioned; the local objective was wrong. Likewise, per-shard clipping with different factors changes gradient direction and is not equivalent to clipping the global vector. Correct distributed math begins with the logical loss and ownership map.

Exercise — Masked microbatches and an averaged all-reduce

Two ranks accumulate two microbatches each. Their token counts are (100,300) and (200,400), with local sum-gradient contributions (50,450) and (400,1200). The collective averages across two ranks. What coefficient should multiply each local sum loss, and what is the resulting gradient? Contrast averaging all four microbatch means.

Show worked solution

The global token count is N=1000 and the total sum gradient is 50+450+400+1200=2100. Each local sum loss receives d/N=2/1000.

g0=(50+450)⋅0.002=1.0g1=(400+1200)⋅0.002=3.2gˉ=1.0+3.22=2.1gmean of means=0.5+1.5+2+34=1.75\begin{aligned}g_0&=(50+450)\cdot0.002=1.0\\g_1&=(400+1200)\cdot0.002=3.2\\\bar g&=\frac{1.0+3.2}{2}=2.1\\g_{\mathrm{mean\ of\ means}}&=\frac{0.5+1.5+2+3}{4}=1.75\end{aligned}g0​g1​gˉ​gmean of means​​=(50+450)⋅0.002=1.0=(400+1200)⋅0.002=3.2=21.0+3.2​=2.1=40.5+1.5+2+3​=1.75​

The 2.1 result optimizes the global token mean. The 1.75 result weights each microbatch equally despite different token counts. No further division by two accumulation steps is needed after the global normalization.

ZeRO's deeper contribution: state is needed at different times

Optimizer moments are needed when a parameter is updated, not by every rank while computing every forward layer. A gradient shard is needed by the rank responsible for that update, not necessarily as a full tensor everywhere. Parameters are needed only for the layers currently executing, plus a controlled prefetch window. ZeRO progressively exploits these differences. The colored bars in the figure distinguish which replication is removed at each stage; they should be read as ownership, not merely compression. [7]

With d ranks and N parameter elements, a simplified DDP all-reduce sends approximately 2(d−1)N/d elements per rank per step. ZeRO-2 can instead reduce-scatter gradients to owners and all-gather updated parameters, giving a similar asymptotic amount under matching widths. ZeRO-3 additionally gathers parameter shards before forward/backward use. If full parameters are freed after forward and gathered again before backward, an idealized accounting gives two parameter all-gathers plus one gradient reduce-scatter: roughly 3(d−1)N/d elements. Actual dtype widths, reuse, buckets and accumulation determine bytes.

This makes the memory/communication trade explicit. ZeRO-3 may support a much larger model or batch but expose more frequent communication. Keeping a parameter unit resident from forward to backward saves a gather while increasing memory. Increasing the unit size reduces startup overhead but raises the peak live allocation. There is no single “ZeRO-3 bandwidth cost” independent of lifetime policy.

FSDP: wrapping granularity defines the live set

A fully sharded unit owns local parameter shards while idle. Before its compute, ranks all-gather the unit; after compute they may reshard it. During backward, parameters are gathered again as needed and gradients reduce-scattered to their owners. Prefetch can materialize the next unit while the current one computes, creating an overlap window but also two live full units. In FSDP1, rate limiting prevents an asynchronous host from queuing more all-gathers than memory can tolerate. [28] [30]

A useful peak-memory approximation is therefore:

Mpeak≈Mpersistent shards+Msaved activations+Mcurrent full parameters+Mprefetched full parameters+Munreduced gradients+Mcollective buffers+Mallocator slack\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{peak}}&\approx M_{\mathrm{persistent\ shards}}+M_{\mathrm{saved\ activations}}\\ &\quad+M_{\mathrm{current\ full\ parameters}}+M_{\mathrm{prefetched\ full\ parameters}}\\ &\quad+M_{\mathrm{unreduced\ gradients}}+M_{\mathrm{collective\ buffers}}+M_{\mathrm{allocator\ slack}}\end{aligned}Mpeak​​≈Mpersistent shards​+Msaved activations​+Mcurrent full parameters​+Mprefetched full parameters​+Munreduced gradients​+Mcollective buffers​+Mallocator slack​​

If a whole model is wrapped as one unit, the full model may materialize at once and much of the intended memory saving disappears. If every tiny tensor is its own unit, communication startup and launch overhead can dominate. Transformer-block units are a common starting point because they align with useful compute windows, but embeddings, huge experts and uneven layers may need different boundaries. The best granularity is a measured compromise.

Sharding also interacts with the optimizer. Elementwise Adam states naturally align with parameter shards. An optimizer that uses a whole-tensor norm or matrix-level transformation may need additional global statistics or a layout that preserves the required dimension. Applying a tensorwise rule independently to arbitrary flattened fragments can change the algorithm. Similarly, global gradient clipping requires the norm over all relevant unique gradient elements; replicated copies must not be counted twice.

Derivation: FSDP memory is determined by parameter lifetimes, not just shard size

Model. A model has N parameters across d data-parallel ranks. Let sw,sg,so be bytes per parameter for working weights, accumulated gradients and optimizer/master state. These persistent states are fully sharded. A materialized parameter unit contains U parameters. A is saved-activation memory and Bbuf is other temporary memory. Assume parameter all-gathers allocate new full buffers while the original shards remain resident; an implementation that aliases buffers must be counted differently. FSDP.

1. Count the persistent baseline. Owning one d-th of each state gives Mbase=N(sw+sg+so)/d. This is only the idle baseline, because the next matrix multiplication needs an executable full parameter unit.

2. Count the maximum simultaneous live set. If the current unit and one prefetched unit are both materialized, the conservative ledger is:

Mpeak≈N(sw+sg+so)d+A+2Usw+BbufWithout prefetch: 2Usw⟶UswSubtract a local shard only when the gather buffer actually aliases it.\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{peak}}&\approx\frac{N(s_w+s_g+s_o)}d+A+2Us_w+B_{\mathrm{buf}}\\ \text{Without prefetch: }&2Us_w\longrightarrow Us_w\\ &\text{Subtract a local shard only when the gather buffer actually aliases it.}\end{aligned}Mpeak​Without prefetch: ​≈dN(sw​+sg​+so​)​+A+2Usw​+Bbuf​2Usw​⟶Usw​Subtract a local shard only when the gather buffer actually aliases it.​

Wrapping the whole model as one unit sets U=N and defeats much of the intended peak-memory saving. Conversely, tiny units lower 2Usw but multiply communication startups.

3. Count communication from the lifetime policy. If weights are gathered once for forward and freed, gathered again for backward, and gradients are reduce-scattered once, each rank moves approximately [(d−1)/d]N(2sw+sg) bytes per optimizer step, excluding optional parameter-update gathers and accumulation-specific behavior. Retaining full parameters from forward to backward removes one gather at a memory cost. The bandwidth expression follows because an all-gather or reduce-scatter contributes (d−1)/d of its logical tensor bytes per rank in the ideal ring accounting.

Example. For N=8 billion, d=8 and a 16-byte persistent state ledger, Mbase=16 GB. If sw=2 bytes and U=0.5 billion, two full units add 2 GB. With A=10 GB and Bbuf=2 GB, the modeled peak is 30 GB. Whole-model units would add 32 GB instead, giving 60 GB. These are decimal totals before allocator effects. The useful optimization variable is the number and size of simultaneously live units, not simply the sharding degree.

Exercise — Trade a gather for memory

Use N=8 billion, d=8, sw=sg=2 bytes. Compute ideal per-rank bytes for two weight all-gathers plus one gradient reduce-scatter. Then compute the savings if weights remain resident and only one all-gather is needed. What additional measurement is needed before adopting the policy?

Show worked solution
V2 gathers+scatter=78⋅8⋅109(2⋅2+2)=42⋅109 bytes/rankVgather+scatter=78⋅8⋅109(2+2)=28⋅109 bytes/rankΔV=14 GB/rank/step\begin{aligned}V_{\mathrm{2\ gathers+scatter}}&=\frac78\cdot8\cdot10^9(2\cdot2+2)=42\cdot10^9\,\mathrm{bytes/rank}\\ V_{\mathrm{gather+scatter}}&=\frac78\cdot8\cdot10^9(2+2)=28\cdot10^9\,\mathrm{bytes/rank}\\ \Delta V&=14\,\mathrm{GB/rank/step}\end{aligned}V2 gathers+scatter​Vgather+scatter​ΔV​=87​⋅8⋅109(2⋅2+2)=42⋅109bytes/rank=87​⋅8⋅109(2+2)=28⋅109bytes/rank=14GB/rank/step​

The retained full parameters increase the live memory set between forward and backward. Measure whether that reduces feasible microbatch size or activation storage enough to offset the communication saving. Also measure exposed rather than total gather time: a fully hidden gather has no immediate latency to recover.

FSDP2 changes the representation and control interface

The historical FSDP paper and wrapper terminology describe FSDP1. Modern FSDP2 exposes a composable fully_shard operation and represents shards per parameter through DTensor, instead of making a flattened parameter the central public representation. It retains the same fundamental need to gather before use and manage lifetimes, while improving how sharding composes with tensor parallelism and other transformations. Implicit prefetch handles common execution orders; explicit prefetch can describe future modules when the default order is insufficient. [29]

Do not transplant FSDP1 configuration names blindly into FSDP2. Wrapping, parameter initialization and memory-management APIs differ; the conceptual question is still how many full parameter groups can be live, which group is prefetched, and when resharding occurs. This distinction matters when reproducing a historical benchmark with a current runtime: the algorithmic family may be the same while the implementation's memory and overlap behavior has changed.

Recomputation and offload are different exchanges

Activation checkpointing exchanges extra computation for fewer saved activations. Offload exchanges transfer time and host/storage capacity for HBM capacity. Prefetch exchanges extra live buffers for overlap. These optimizations compete for the same memory budget, so applying all three maximally is rarely optimal.

For an offloaded unit of D bytes and available prefetch slack C seconds, complete hiding requires effective transfer bandwidth at least D/C, plus enough HBM for the prefetched object. A 2 GB unit with a 10 ms window would need 200 GB/s useful bandwidth—unrealistic for many CPU/GPU paths. NVMe can make a model feasible while remaining far too slow for a short per-layer window. ZeRO-Infinity's scheduling matters because the hierarchy is useful only when transfers can be overlapped, batched or amortized. [8]

When replication is preferable

If a model fits and there are many independent inference requests, independent serving replicas avoid inter-device communication on each token. Training data parallelism synchronizes gradients; serving replication usually does not. The shared name can hide this major difference.

Tensor parallelism: split operators and pay per-layer communication

For an MLP Y=φ(XW1)W2, split W1 by output columns and W2 by matching input rows. Each rank computes its own intermediate activation and partial final output. Summing those outputs reconstructs Y. Megatron exploits this arrangement to avoid a collective between the first matrix product and pointwise nonlinearity. [2]

W1=[W1,0⋯W1,p−1],W2=[W2,0⋮W2,p−1]Y=∑iϕ(XW1,i)W2,i\begin{aligned}W_1&=\begin{bmatrix}W_{1,0}&\cdots&W_{1,p-1}\end{bmatrix},\quad W_2=\begin{bmatrix}W_{2,0}\\\vdots\\W_{2,p-1}\end{bmatrix}\\Y&=\sum_i\phi(XW_{1,i})W_{2,i}\end{aligned}W1​Y​=[W1,0​​⋯​W1,p−1​​],W2​=​W2,0​⋮W2,p−1​​​=i∑​ϕ(XW1,i​)W2,i​​

Attention heads can also be partitioned. Grouped-query attention complicates the mapping when there are fewer KV heads than TP ranks; replication or special partitioning may be required. Vocabulary-parallel embeddings and output logits avoid gathering a huge vocabulary tensor, but loss and sampling still need distributed coordination.

TP lowers per-device compute and weight residency, yet adds synchronization many times per token. At small decode batch sizes, a matrix becomes so narrow that adding ranks yields little compute benefit while collective latency remains. Keep frequently communicating TP groups within a fast fabric when feasible; topology should determine the practical degree.

Megatron's algebra explains the f/g boundaries

Suppose X has shape T×h, W1 is h×4h and W2 is 4h×h. Splitting W1's columns gives each rank a disjoint part of the hidden expansion. The pointwise nonlinearity can run independently on each part. W2 is split by matching rows, producing partial outputs that must be summed. If W1 were split by rows instead, ranks would create partial sums before the nonlinearity and would have to communicate there, because φ(a+b) generally differs from φ(a)+φ(b). This is why the two-layer block, not an arbitrary matrix, is the useful partitioning unit. [2]

Let dY be the upstream gradient. After the row-parallel second GEMM, every rank needs the same dY to compute its local weight and hidden gradients. Before the column-parallel first GEMM, contributions to dX from all hidden shards must be summed. The original f operator is identity in forward and all-reduce in backward; g is all-reduce in forward and identity in backward. These are custom distributed-autograd semantics for the chosen replicated layout, not an instruction to differentiate a redundant all-reduce naïvely on every copy.

Zi=ϕ(XW1,i),Yi=ZiW2,i,Y=∑iYi∂L∂W2,i=Zi⊤dYGi=(dYW2,i⊤)⊙ϕ′(XW1,i)∂L∂W1,i=X⊤Gi,∂L∂X=∑iGiW1,i⊤\begin{aligned}Z_i&=\phi(XW_{1,i}),\quad Y_i=Z_iW_{2,i},\quad Y=\sum_iY_i\\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{2,i}}&=Z_i^\top\mathrm dY\\ G_i&=(\mathrm dY W_{2,i}^\top)\odot\phi'(XW_{1,i})\\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{1,i}}&=X^\top G_i,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=\sum_iG_iW_{1,i}^\top\end{aligned}Zi​∂W2,i​∂L​Gi​∂W1,i​∂L​​=ϕ(XW1,i​),Yi​=Zi​W2,i​,Y=i∑​Yi​=Zi⊤​dY=(dYW2,i⊤​)⊙ϕ′(XW1,i​)=X⊤Gi​,∂X∂L​=i∑​Gi​W1,i⊤​​

For a gated MLP, gate and up projections must use matching hidden partitions so their elementwise product is local; the down projection then sums those hidden contributions. Attention partitions heads so each local head can compute its own attention before the output projection. With GQA, Hkv may be smaller than the TP degree, forcing KV replication or a different layout. A model's head counts therefore constrain which parallel degrees remain efficient.

Derivation: Megatron communication boundaries follow the chain rule

Shapes and layout. Let X∈ℝ^(T×h), W₁∈ℝ^(h×f), W₂∈ℝ^(f×h), Z=φ(XW₁) and Y=ZW₂. Partition f across p ranks. Each rank i stores W₁,i's columns and the matching W₂,i rows; X and Y are logical replicated boundary tensors. φ acts elementwise. The forward sum is Y=ΣᵢZiW₂,i. Megatron-LM.

1. Take a differential. Define G=∂L/∂Y. For each rank, dY contains dZiW₂,i+Zi dW₂,i. The Frobenius inner-product identity ⟨G,AB⟩=⟨GBᵀ,A⟩ gives the local adjoints:

∂L∂W2,i=Zi⊤G,∂L∂Zi=GW2,i⊤Hi=(GW2,i⊤)⊙ϕ′(XW1,i)∂L∂W1,i=X⊤Hi,∂L∂X=∑iHiW1,i⊤\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{2,i}}&=Z_i^\top G,\quad\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_i}=GW_{2,i}^\top\\ H_i&=(GW_{2,i}^\top)\odot\phi'(XW_{1,i})\\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{1,i}}&=X^\top H_i,\quad\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=\sum_iH_iW_{1,i}^\top\end{aligned}∂W2,i​∂L​Hi​∂W1,i​∂L​​=Zi⊤​G,∂Zi​∂L​=GW2,i⊤​=(GW2,i⊤​)⊙ϕ′(XW1,i​)=X⊤Hi​,∂X∂L​=i∑​Hi​W1,i⊤​​

The last sum is unavoidable because every hidden shard depends on the same logical X. The forward output sum and backward input-gradient sum are the two communication boundaries; no reduction is needed between W₁ and φ because each hidden coordinate is completely local.

2. Explain the custom f/g operators. At the first boundary, forward replication acts as identity on each local copy but backward must add contributions. At the second boundary, forward adds partial Y values, while backward supplies the same logical G to each contributor. Replicated copies represent one logical tensor/loss, not p independent losses. Naively differentiating redundant reductions and summing duplicate losses can introduce an unwanted factor p.

3. Why another partition communicates earlier. Splitting W₁ along its reduction dimension creates partial XiW₁,i that must be summed before φ. In general φ(a+b)≠φ(a)+φ(b): for ReLU, a=1,b=−1 gives ReLU(a+b)=0 but ReLU(a)+ReLU(b)=1. The valid partition therefore follows the algebra of the entire block, not the visual shape of an individual matrix.

Exercise — Compute a two-rank MLP gradient by hand

Let X=[1,2], W₁,0=[1,0]ᵀ, W₁,1=[0,1]ᵀ, φ be identity, W₂,0=[3,4], W₂,1=[5,6], and upstream G=[1,−1]. Find Y, both W₂ gradients, both W₁ gradients, and the reduced X gradient.

Show worked solution
Z0=1,Z1=2,Y=[3,4]+2[5,6]=[13,16]dW2,0=[1,−1],dW2,1=2[1,−1]=[2,−2]H0=[1,−1][3,4]⊤=−1,H1=[1,−1][5,6]⊤=−1dW1,0=dW1,1=X⊤(−1)=[−1,−2]⊤dX0=[−1,0],dX1=[0,−1]dX=dX0+dX1=[−1,−1]\begin{aligned}Z_0&=1,\quad Z_1=2,\quad Y=[3,4]+2[5,6]=[13,16]\\ \mathrm dW_{2,0}&=[1,-1],\quad\mathrm dW_{2,1}=2[1,-1]=[2,-2]\\ H_0&=[1,-1][3,4]^\top=-1,\quad H_1=[1,-1][5,6]^\top=-1\\ \mathrm dW_{1,0}&=\mathrm dW_{1,1}=X^\top(-1)=[-1,-2]^\top\\ \mathrm dX_0&=[-1,0],\quad\mathrm dX_1=[0,-1]\\ \mathrm dX&=\mathrm dX_0+\mathrm dX_1=[-1,-1]\end{aligned}Z0​dW2,0​H0​dW1,0​dX0​dX​=1,Z1​=2,Y=[3,4]+2[5,6]=[13,16]=[1,−1],dW2,1​=2[1,−1]=[2,−2]=[1,−1][3,4]⊤=−1,H1​=[1,−1][5,6]⊤=−1=dW1,1​=X⊤(−1)=[−1,−2]⊤=[−1,0],dX1​=[0,−1]=dX0​+dX1​=[−1,−1]​

The output contributions sum in forward and input-gradient contributions sum in backward. The weight gradients remain local because their parameters are disjoint.

Vocabulary parallelism avoids a huge gather

The output vocabulary projection can be partitioned by vocabulary range. Each rank computes local logits. Training cross-entropy does not require gathering the entire vocabulary: reduce the maximum for stable exponentiation, reduce the sum of exponentials, and obtain the target-token logit from its owning shard. This moves a small number of scalars per token instead of V logits. Sampling is more complicated: exact top-k or nucleus sampling needs enough distributed information to identify the global candidate set, and naïve local truncation can change the distribution.

Derivation: exact vocabulary-parallel cross-entropy without gathering logits

Setup. One token's vocabulary logits zj are partitioned into disjoint sets Vi. The target token is y, owned by exactly one rank. Cross-entropy is L=log(Σj exp zj)−zy. The objective requires a sum and a target value, not the full logit vector on every device. This follows directly from the output-layer partition in Megatron-LM.

1. Stabilize globally. Each rank computes its local maximum mi. An all-reduce MAX gives m=maxi mi. Now all exponents exp(zj−m) are at most one. Each rank sums si=Σj∈Vi exp(zj−m); an all-reduce SUM gives s=Σi si. The owner supplies zy while other ranks contribute zero to a target-logit reduction.

L=m+log⁡s−zypj=exp⁡(zj−m)s,j∈Vi∂L∂zj=pj−1[j=y]\begin{aligned}L&=m+\log s-z_y\\p_j&=\frac{\exp(z_j-m)}s,\quad j\in V_i\\\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}&=p_j-\mathbf1[j=y]\end{aligned}Lpj​∂zj​∂L​​=m+logs−zy​=sexp(zj​−m)​,j∈Vi​=pj​−1[j=y]​

2. Show why the max introduces no extra model term. Since log Σexp(zj)=m+logΣexp(zj−m) for any common finite m, differentiating the two occurrences of m cancels: dm−(Σjpj)dm=0. The remaining derivative is Σjpj dzj. A fused implementation can directly use pj−one_hot(y), including at ties in the maximum, instead of treating a choice of stable offset as a learned operation.

3. Communication scaling. For T tokens this exchanges T maxima, T sums and T target values, rather than T×V logits. The local logit and weight gradients still require their normal matrix work. Exact softmax sampling has another information requirement; this training loss derivation does not justify truncating each rank's candidates independently for top-p sampling.

Example. Partition logits [0,ln2] and [ln3,ln4], with target the third class. Z=1+2+3+4=10, so the probability vector is [0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4] and L=ln(10/3)≈1.204. The local gradients are [0.1,0.2] and [−0.7,0.4]. Two reduced scalars plus the target logit reproduce the same loss as a gathered softmax in real arithmetic.

Exercise — A stable distributed log-sum-exp

Two ranks hold logits [1000,1001] and [999,1002]; the target is the second class. Write the stable denominator, loss and target probability without exponentiating 1002.

Show worked solution

The global maximum is m=1002. Shifted logits are [−2,−1] and [−3,0].

s=e−2+e−1+e−3+1≈1.5530018ptarget=e−1s≈0.2368828L=1002+ln⁡s−1001=1+ln⁡s≈1.4401897\begin{aligned}s&=e^{-2}+e^{-1}+e^{-3}+1\approx1.5530018\\p_{\mathrm{target}}&=\frac{e^{-1}}s\approx0.2368828\\L&=1002+\ln s-1001=1+\ln s\approx1.4401897\end{aligned}sptarget​L​=e−2+e−1+e−3+1≈1.5530018=se−1​≈0.2368828=1002+lns−1001=1+lns≈1.4401897​

Each rank exponentiates only nonpositive shifted logits. The loss is invariant to the original common large offset, avoiding numerical overflow without changing the probability distribution.

Predict the TP scaling knee

Let a layer have compute time C1 on one device and exposed collective cost A(p) on p devices. An optimistic model is C1/p + A(p), but narrow GEMMs often scale worse than 1/p. Once the compute saved by another rank is smaller than its extra communication and kernel inefficiency, latency rises. Decode reaches this knee early because T can be small; prefill has larger matrices and can tolerate a larger TP degree.

For a rough replicated-boundary transformer, there are two forward reductions per layer, each on a T×h activation. Their bytes scale with T·h, whereas dense-layer work scales with T·h². Larger hidden widths can therefore have a better compute/communication ratio; increasing batch does not remove the latency of each collective, but can amortize startup and improve matrix efficiency. This explains why a TP degree appropriate for a large model or prefill may be poor for a smaller model's interactive decode.

From manual layouts to compiled layouts

Mesh-TensorFlow expresses tensor dimensions and device-mesh dimensions explicitly; distributing a reduction dimension implies a reduction, while distributing an output dimension implies a sharded result. GSPMD propagates limited sharding annotations through a computation graph and inserts communication at incompatible boundaries. Alpa adds search across inter-operator stages and intra-operator layouts with a cost model. [31] [32] [15]

The common abstraction is a distributed tensor type: shape plus ownership. Compiler convenience does not eliminate the physical tradeoff. A locally attractive operator layout can force an expensive redistribution into its successor. A useful planner minimizes the graph's total exposed time subject to memory and topology, rather than choosing the fastest isolated partition for every operator.

Pipeline parallelism: scheduling becomes the algorithm

GPipe splits model depth across devices and divides a batch into microbatches. Forward and backward passes are scheduled in phases, with synchronous updates. This reduces weight residency, but storing activations and filling/draining the pipeline costs memory and idle time. [4]

PipeDream explores steadier forward/backward interleaving and weight-version management. PipeDream-2BW limits weight buffering while preserving its update semantics. These semantics must be checked before claiming equivalence to ordinary synchronous SGD. The phrase “1F1B” specifies a schedule pattern, not every detail of the optimizer. [5] [6]

Megatron’s interleaved pipeline places multiple model chunks on each device to reduce bubble time, at the cost of more communication and scheduling complexity. Combining TP, PP, and DP gives a three-dimensional mapping onto the cluster. [3]

Tcompletion≈(m+p−1)tfbubble≈p−1m+p−1Balanced forward pipeline: p stages, m microbatches, stage time t.Backward asymmetry, communication, memory limits and imbalance omitted.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{completion}}&\approx(m+p-1)t\\f_{\mathrm{bubble}}&\approx\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}\\&\text{Balanced forward pipeline: }p\text{ stages, }m\text{ microbatches, stage time }t.\\&\text{Backward asymmetry, communication, memory limits and imbalance omitted.}\end{aligned}Tcompletion​fbubble​​≈(m+p−1)t≈m+p−1p−1​Balanced forward pipeline: p stages, m microbatches, stage time t.Backward asymmetry, communication, memory limits and imbalance omitted.​

Increasing m reduces the bubble fraction but may create inefficient tiny microbatches or require a larger global batch. Equal layer counts do not ensure equal time: embeddings, attention at different sequence lengths, and MoE load can unbalance stages.

GPipe to interleaved 1F1B: the changing bottleneck

The naïve schedule sends an entire batch through one stage at a time; devices wait for work that has not arrived. GPipe splits the batch into m microbatches and accumulates gradients before a synchronous update. In its fill-drain form, all forward microbatches precede backward. This gives simple optimizer semantics but can require retaining many activations, motivating rematerialization. [4]

For p balanced stages with forward time f and backward time b per microbatch, an ideal flush schedule takes approximately (m+p−1)(f+b). Useful busy time is m(f+b), giving bubble fraction (p−1)/(m+p−1). With p=8,m=32 the simplified idle fraction is 7/39≈17.9%; with m=128 it is 7/135≈5.2%. The arithmetic is useful, but increasing m while holding global batch fixed shrinks each microbatch and can reduce GEMM efficiency.

A noninterleaved 1F1B schedule performs warmup forwards, then alternates forward and backward, then drains. By retiring activations sooner, it reduces the live activation count relative to a long forward-only phase. It does not automatically eliminate the fill/drain bubble. Nor does “1F1B” specify whether weight updates are synchronous or stale: that belongs to the optimizer/version protocol.

PipeDream's weight stashing ensures that a microbatch's backward uses the appropriate version for its earlier forward in an asynchronous pipeline. Bounded-version descendants such as PipeDream-2BW reduce storage and alter update timing. These are not merely interchangeable memory optimizations for exact synchronous SGD. Any comparison should state the versioning semantics and whether convergence was measured at equal processed tokens and target quality. [5] [6]

Megatron's interleaving assigns v smaller model chunks to each device. The figure's dark/light blocks are different chunks, not different physical GPUs. Smaller effective stages reduce the bubble, roughly by v in idealized analysis, but produce more activation transfers and more scheduling events. The network and microbatch efficiency determine whether the saved idle time exceeds those costs. A device can own nonadjacent depth ranges, so simple layer-count balancing is insufficient. [3]

Stage balance is a maximum, not an average

If stage times are t1,…,tp, the steady pipeline rate is limited by max(ti). Moving a layer from the slowest stage can improve throughput even when it slightly increases total communication. Embeddings, the output projection, MoE routing and different recomputation choices create unequal work. The best partition is based on profiled time and memory at the intended microbatch/sequence shape.

Virtual chunks complicate memory lifetime: a device may hold activations for several noncontiguous stages, and prefetch/communication buffers may overlap. A valid schedule must satisfy data dependencies, parameter-version requirements and allocation limits simultaneously. Schedule diagrams are therefore compact proofs of feasible ordering, not merely illustrations of “more overlap.”

Derivation: pipeline bubbles, microbatch count, and stage imbalance

Balanced synchronous model. There are p pipeline stages and m microbatches per optimizer step. A forward microbatch takes tf on every stage; its backward takes tb. Ignore transfers and assume the fill/drain GPipe schedule executes all forward work before the backward wave. Weights remain fixed across the m microbatches. GPipe and 1F1B/weight-version work motivate the scheduling distinction.

1. Count stage-time slots. The first forward microbatch takes p slots to cross the pipeline, then each of the remaining m−1 exits one slot later. Thus Tforward=(m+p−1)tf. The reverse backward wave has the same count with tb.

Tstep=(m+p−1)(tf+tb)Tuseful=m(tf+tb)u=mm+p−1,fbubble=p−1m+p−1\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{step}}&=(m+p-1)(t_f+t_b)\\T_{\mathrm{useful}}&=m(t_f+t_b)\\u&=\frac m{m+p-1},\quad f_{\mathrm{bubble}}=\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}\end{aligned}Tstep​Tuseful​u​=(m+p−1)(tf​+tb​)=m(tf​+tb​)=m+p−1m​,fbubble​=m+p−1p−1​​

To make bubbles at most ε, solve (p−1)/(m+p−1)≤ε. Multiplying positive denominators gives m≥(p−1)(1/ε−1). With p=8 and ε=0.1, at least 63 microbatches are required in this simplified schedule. Increasing m is constrained by global batch, microbatch efficiency and the optimizer's statistical regime.

2. Separate activation memory from bubble length. GPipe may retain forward activations for all m microbatches before backward starts. A noninterleaved 1F1B schedule begins backward earlier, so activation residency can scale with pipeline depth rather than m for early stages. Its benefit does not require an identical reduction in arithmetic or asymptotic bubble fraction. The exact count depends on stage position and warmup.

3. Introduce imbalance. In a forward-only pipeline with stage times ti, a deterministic m-microbatch makespan is at least Σi ti+(m−1)maxi ti. The sum is the first microbatch's traversal; the maximum is the bottleneck stage's minimum spacing between completions. With stages [1,1,1,3] ms and m=8, this is 6+7×3=27 ms. Redistributing the same 6 ms total work to [1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5] gives 6+7×1.5=16.5 ms. Equal parameter counts are not evidence of equal stage times.

Exercise — Choose enough microbatches without confusing utilization and speedup

A balanced p=4 GPipe pipeline has tf=2 ms, tb=4 ms and m=12. Calculate step time, per-stage utilization and bubble fraction. What is the minimum m for at most 5% bubbles under this model?

Show worked solution
T=(12+4−1)(2+4)=90 msTuseful=12⋅6=72 msu=7290=0.8,fbubble=0.2=20%m≥(4−1)(10.05−1)=57\begin{aligned}T&=(12+4-1)(2+4)=90\,\mathrm{ms}\\T_{\mathrm{useful}}&=12\cdot6=72\,\mathrm{ms}\\u&=\frac{72}{90}=0.8,\quad f_{\mathrm{bubble}}=0.2=20\%\\m&\ge(4-1)\left(\frac1{0.05}-1\right)=57\end{aligned}TTuseful​um​=(12+4−1)(2+4)=90ms=12⋅6=72ms=9072​=0.8,fbubble​=0.2=20%≥(4−1)(0.051​−1)=57​

The 80% utilization is relative to this pipeline's ideal schedule, not a speedup over one accelerator running the entire model. That comparison additionally requires the single-device layer times, memory feasibility and communication overhead. The global optimization batch may also make m=57 undesirable or impossible.

Zero Bubble → DualPipe / DualPipeV

Zero Bubble separates backward work for input gradients from work for parameter gradients. Input gradients unblock the previous stage; weight gradients can often be delayed into otherwise idle slots. Memory limits and optimizer synchronization still constrain a realizable schedule. [13]

DualPipe combines bidirectional scheduling and carefully implemented overlap of forward/backward computation with communication. DualPipeV changes the placement into a V-shaped schedule. Their repository explicitly requires a model-specific overlapped forward/backward implementation: importing a schedule is insufficient to obtain the reported overlap. Buffer and parameter residency also differ from a basic 1F1B schedule. [14]

Zero Bubble: split a backward pass by its dependency role

For Y=XW, backward computes dX=dYWᵀ and dW=XᵀdY. The previous pipeline stage needs dX immediately to continue; the optimizer needs dW only before the update. Treating both as one indivisible backward operation places weight-gradient work unnecessarily on the inter-stage critical path. Zero Bubble separates input-gradient work B from weight-gradient work W and uses delayed W to fill otherwise idle slots. [13]

This is a change in the dependency graph exposed to the scheduler. It does not remove dW or reduce training FLOPs. Delaying W retains X and relevant gradients for longer, increasing live memory. The original handcrafted schedules assume comparable F/B/W durations for intuition; the more realistic scheduler profiles unequal times and respects memory constraints. Some schedules improve utilization at the same memory budget, while more aggressive schedules require more memory.

Optimizer synchronization remains a boundary: all required gradients must be valid, and global clipping or overflow checks may need a collective. The paper's post-validation approach rearranges that synchronization, with recovery behavior if validation fails. “Zero bubble” should therefore be read with the schedule's assumptions, not as a guarantee that every real iteration has no idle time from imbalance, network delays or failures.

DualPipe and FLUX attack different overlap granularities

DualPipe operates across pipeline microbatches and within a customized forward/backward implementation. It overlaps attention, expert work, dispatch/combine and pipeline communication where the graph permits, with bidirectional scheduling to reduce exposed gaps. Its V-shaped descendant changes chunk placement and memory tradeoffs. The repository requires a model-specific overlapped forward/backward function; the schedule alone is insufficient. [14] [34]

FLUX instead decomposes tensor-parallel communication and GEMM into fine tiles and fuses their handling, allowing a compute tile to proceed once its required operand tile is ready rather than waiting for a whole collective. This can expose overlap between nominally dependent operations. It still pays for readiness signaling, memory access and resource contention; the relevant result is reduced exposed latency, not communication disappearing. [33]

The general principle is to find the smallest useful dependency. An entire all-gather may precede a GEMM in a coarse graph, but each GEMM tile needs only some gathered rows. An entire backward may precede the previous layer's backward in a coarse graph, but only dX is urgent. Research progress often comes from exposing that finer structure while keeping kernels large enough to remain efficient.

Long-context parallelism: several meanings of “sequence parallel”

Megatron sequence parallelism shards sequence-local operations such as normalization/dropout around tensor-parallel regions, reducing replicated activation storage. It should be distinguished from distributing a whole long attention computation across devices. [9]

Ulysses begins with sequence shards, then uses all-to-all to redistribute into head shards with the full sequence available per assigned head. After attention, a reverse all-to-all restores sequence ownership. The number and arrangement of heads, especially KV heads, constrain the practical partition. [10]

Ring Attention keeps local queries and circulates key/value blocks. Attention over each block is merged using numerically stable online softmax statistics. Computation can overlap block transfers when blocks are large enough. Long sequences increase available compute per transfer; small blocks or poor networks expose communication. [11]

m=max⁡(ma,mb)l=ema−mla+emb−mlbo=ema−moa+emb−mobYattention=ol(unnormalized weighted-value sums oa,ob)\begin{aligned}m&=\max(m_a,m_b)\\l&=e^{m_a-m}l_a+e^{m_b-m}l_b\\o&=e^{m_a-m}o_a+e^{m_b-m}o_b\\Y_{\mathrm{attention}}&=\frac ol\quad\text{(unnormalized weighted-value sums }o_a,o_b\text{)}\end{aligned}mloYattention​​=max(ma​,mb​)=ema​−mla​+emb​−mlb​=ema​−moa​+emb​−mob​=lo​(unnormalized weighted-value sums oa​,ob​)​

USP combines Ulysses-style and ring-style dimensions, matching the all-to-all-heavy part to faster local connectivity and extending sequence partitioning across another dimension. Causal attention needs load balancing: early query positions attend fewer keys than late positions. Contiguous equal-length shards can therefore have unequal work. [12]

These methods distribute exact attention computation in their mathematical formulation. They do not remove its quadratic arithmetic for full attention. Sparse attention and recurrent-state models change that separate dimension of the problem.

Sequence parallelism is an ownership vocabulary, not one algorithm

In Megatron's 2022 sequence parallelism, normalization and dropout can operate independently on tokens. Replicating those activations across the TP group wastes memory. Replace an all-reduce boundary with reduce-scatter to retain sequence shards, then all-gather before a tensor-parallel region that needs the full token dimension. All-reduce itself decomposes into these two operations, so the change can remove redundant activation storage without simply adding a full new collective. Backward uses conjugate ownership transformations. [9]

This does not mean each attention head now computes only its local context and ignores remote tokens. The attention ownership is determined by the TP region. The paper also analyzes selective activation recomputation: recomputing inexpensive attention intermediates can save memory without recomputing every large GEMM. Sequence sharding and recomputation address different terms in the live-memory budget and can be combined.

Ulysses uses a different transformation. With p ranks, each initially owns S/p tokens for H heads. An all-to-all redistributes Q/K/V so each rank owns all S tokens for H/p heads. Local attention is then ordinary full-sequence attention on those heads, and the reverse all-to-all restores sequence shards. The red arrows in the figure are therefore a distributed transpose of ownership, not an approximate attention operation. [10]

For equal Q/K/V dimensions, each rank holds O(BSHd/p) elements and sends a fraction (p−1)/p of those during a redistribution. Forward includes the Q/K/V transpose and the output transpose; backward has corresponding exchanges. A practical implementation must pack tensors in layouts that keep both communication and the local attention kernel efficient. The theoretical payload advantage can be eroded by transpose kernels, padding or small messages.

Head divisibility constrains Ulysses. GQA has many query heads but few KV heads; beyond Hkv ranks, an implementation needs replication or a modified grouping. A topology with efficient all-to-all is also important. A method whose asymptotic volume decreases per rank is not necessarily fast on a network with poor all-to-all bisection.

Ring Attention: exactness is the softmax merge, speed is an overlap condition

A rank retains local Q and rotates K/V blocks through its neighbors. For each block it computes a partial attention state and merges it using the stable maximum/sum/weighted-output recurrence given above. Block order can change without changing the exact real-number attention expression. Numerical rounding may differ; masks and position handling must still match the original model. [11]

The important storage result is that all remote K/V need not coexist in memory. A rank holds its local state and a small number of in-flight blocks. The important performance condition is that compute on one block lasts long enough to hide transfer of the next. For a simplified full-attention block of c queries and c keys at head width d, QK and PV require about 4c²d FLOPs. Transferring K and V requires 2cds bytes where s is bytes per value.

Tcompute≈4c2dC,Ttransfer≈α+2cdsβc≥sC2βfor full overlap, ignoring αs=2  (BF16)⟹c≥Cβ\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{compute}}&\approx\frac{4c^2d}{C},\quad T_{\mathrm{transfer}}\approx\alpha+\frac{2cds}{\beta}\\c&\ge\frac{sC}{2\beta}\quad\text{for full overlap, ignoring }\alpha\\s&=2\;\text{(BF16)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c\ge\frac C\beta\end{aligned}Tcompute​cs​≈C4c2d​,Ttransfer​≈α+β2cds​≥2βsC​for full overlap, ignoring α=2(BF16)⟹c≥βC​​

This is a minimum block size condition, not a promise of zero overhead for any context. Fast arithmetic and a slow inter-node link make the required block larger. Tiny blocks increase startups and expose communication; huge blocks increase temporary memory and can hurt local-kernel scheduling. The paper's analysis considers forward/backward and full transformer memory, so a per-attention-block bound should not be mistaken for the complete implementation's minimum context.

Derivation: the online-softmax state is sufficient and associative

Setup. For one query, let scores sj=q·kj/√d and values vj be partitioned into disjoint blocks. Exact attention is o=(Σj exp(sj)vj)/(Σj exp(sj)). A rank must merge contributions while retaining only a small state. In real arithmetic, the following state exactly represents all processed keys. Floating-point summation order can still alter rounding. Ring Attention.

1. Define one block's state. For block A define mA=maxj∈A sj, lA=Σj∈A exp(sj−mA), and uA=Σj∈A exp(sj−mA)vj. Store u as an unnormalized numerator. It is not yet the output average.

2. Put two blocks on one scale. Let m=max(mA,mB). Because exp(sj−m)=exp(sj−mA)exp(mA−m) for j∈A, both sum and numerator rescale by the same factor:

l=emA−mlA+emB−mlBu=emA−muA+emB−muBo=ul\begin{aligned}l&=e^{m_A-m}l_A+e^{m_B-m}l_B\\u&=e^{m_A-m}u_A+e^{m_B-m}u_B\\o&=\frac ul\end{aligned}luo​=emA​−mlA​+emB​−mlB​=emA​−muA​+emB​−muB​=lu​​

3. Prove order independence. Every merged state satisfies exp(m)l=Σprocessed exp(sj) and exp(m)u=Σprocessed exp(sj)vj. These quantities are simply sums over the union of processed keys. Therefore merging (A∪B) with C or A with (B∪C) represents the same numerator and denominator. The maximum changes only their common scale. This is the mathematical reason blocks can travel around a ring without gathering all K/V simultaneously.

Mask and empty-block details. Masked positions contribute zero, corresponding to score −∞. An entirely masked block should use an identity/empty state; blindly evaluating exp(−∞−(−∞)) produces NaN. Correct kernels guard that case. Causal ownership permutations must preserve absolute positions and the mask. If dropout is used in training, the same logical position-pair must receive the intended random mask regardless of processing order.

Example. Block A has score 0, value 2; B has score ln3, value 10. Their states are (0,1,2) and (ln3,1,10). With m=ln3, the scale factor for A is 1/3: l=4/3, u=32/3, so o=8. This equals (1×2+3×10)/(1+3). Averaging the two block outputs would incorrectly give 6.

Add block C with score ln2 and value −1 to the example. First merge B and C, then merge A. Compute the final output and verify it from the unpartitioned expression.

Show worked solution

For B∪C, use maximum ln3. The factors are 1 for B and 2/3 for C.

lBC=1+23=53,uBC=10+23(−1)=283l=53+13=2,u=283+23=10o=102=5odirect=1⋅2+3⋅10+2(−1)1+3+2=306=5\begin{aligned}l_{BC}&=1+\frac23=\frac53,\quad u_{BC}=10+\frac23(-1)=\frac{28}3\\l&=\frac53+\frac13=2,\quad u=\frac{28}3+\frac23=10\\o&=\frac{10}2=5\\o_{\mathrm{direct}}&=\frac{1\cdot2+3\cdot10+2(-1)}{1+3+2}=\frac{30}6=5\end{aligned}lBC​loodirect​​=1+32​=35​,uBC​=10+32​(−1)=328​=35​+31​=2,u=328​+32​=10=210​=5=1+3+21⋅2+3⋅10+2(−1)​=630​=5​

The different processing order preserves the same scaled sums. The outputs of individual blocks are not additive; their denominators carry essential probability mass.

Causal balancing and hybrid USP

With causal attention, an early query block attends fewer key blocks than a late query block. Assigning contiguous equal-length query ranges to ranks can leave early ranks idle while late ranks compute nearly the whole history. Balanced ownership can pair early and late sequence blocks on the same rank or use a zigzag assignment. The mask and absolute position mapping must be preserved across this permutation.

USP composes an all-to-all dimension with a ring dimension. Use the fast local fabric for a Ulysses-style transpose, then circulate blocks across another dimension to exceed head-count or local-domain limits. This is a layout composition: the product of dimensions determines the context-parallel group, while each dimension has its own communication pattern. It provides choices for GQA, long contexts and hierarchical topology, rather than a universally best hybrid degree. [12]

The limitation shared by these exact context-parallel methods is arithmetic: full attention still performs quadratic work in S. A million-token sequence made feasible in memory may remain expensive in time and energy. Sparse attention, sliding windows or recurrent state change the mathematical operation; context parallelism distributes the chosen operation. These research areas should be compared on separate axes before composing them.

Expert parallelism and overlap

Expert parallelism assigns different MoE weights to different ranks. Dispatch sends token activations to selected experts; combine returns weighted outputs. With T tokens, top-k routing, hidden width h, and s bytes per activation element, a first-order total payload for dispatch plus combine is 2Tkhs bytes before topology and local-route savings.

Unlike a balanced all-reduce, MoE communication follows a changing routing matrix. One hot expert can stall the batch. Expert replication, topology-aware placement, grouped GEMMs, and dispatch/compute overlap address different parts of this problem. DeepEP supplies communication primitives; an expert load balancer supplies placement policy. Version-specific capabilities matter. [22]

Overlapping operations removes exposed communication only when dependencies permit it and resources do not conflict. A transfer and a GEMM may compete for SMs, HBM, or PCIe bandwidth. Measure the combined timeline; adding their isolated peak rates assumes independence that may not exist.

Expert routing is a time-varying sparse traffic matrix

In dense TP, the collective pattern is largely fixed by tensor shapes. In expert parallelism, routing decides V[i,j] at runtime: how many token vectors on source i must be processed by experts on destination j. Top-k duplicates a token into k assignments; several assignments may target experts on the same node, enabling hierarchical dispatch that sends the token once across a slow boundary and fans it out locally. The reverse combine must restore token order and accumulate the routed contributions correctly. [22] [34]

This creates three distinct balancing problems. Statistical balancing encourages the learned router to use experts appropriately. Placement balancing maps experts or replicas to devices. Execution balancing schedules routed batches and communication. A uniform mean token count is insufficient: the busiest expert/rank determines the tail of a synchronous MoE layer. Redundant replicas can reduce hotspots but consume memory and require consistent weights; a changed placement can also invalidate dispatch metadata.

Grouped GEMM combines many expert matrices with different row counts. Padding gives regular shapes but wastes work; dropless execution preserves all assignments but must handle irregular dimensions and buffers. Token sorting and permutation are part of the cost. At low batch, latency may be dominated by dispatch startup and tiny expert GEMMs; at high batch, bandwidth and skew dominate. These regimes motivate separate low-latency and throughput-oriented communication implementations.

A quantitative overlap test for an MoE layer

Let expert compute be C, dispatch/combine duration N, and independent attention/shared-expert work A that can be scheduled concurrently. A naïve execution is A+N+C. A better schedule can hide parts of N under A or other microbatches, but routing dependencies mean an expert cannot process tokens that have not arrived. Chunked arrival lets a destination begin on ready token groups while later groups are in flight, exchanging more scheduling/signaling for smaller exposed delay.

Measure p95/p99 per-rank layer time and routed-token counts together. A high average all-to-all bandwidth can coexist with a slow tail if one destination receives most work. Likewise, reserving many SMs for communication can improve N while worsening C. Tune the combined step time, not the isolated communication benchmark. The MoE guide develops expert placement, capacity and offload in greater detail.

Derivation: expert all-to-all is bounded by traffic cuts, not average bandwidth

Notation and conservation. Let Vij be the bytes that source rank i must send to destination j after routing. In a synchronous dispatch, all required data must arrive before the last dependent expert finishes. A sender with useful injection rate bi cannot transmit ΣjVij bytes in less than that total divided by bi. The same reasoning applies to receiver rate cj and every physical network cut.

Tdispatch≥max⁡{max⁡i∑jVijbi,  max⁡j∑iVijcj,  max⁡cut∑i∈left,j∈rightVijBcut}\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{dispatch}}&\ge\max\left\{\max_i\frac{\sum_j V_{ij}}{b_i},\;\max_j\frac{\sum_i V_{ij}}{c_j},\;\max_{\mathrm{cut}}\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathrm{left},j\in\mathrm{right}}V_{ij}}{B_{\mathrm{cut}}}\right\}\end{aligned}Tdispatch​​≥max{imax​bi​∑j​Vij​​,jmax​cj​∑i​Vij​​,cutmax​Bcut​∑i∈left,j∈right​Vij​​}​

A cut bound counts traffic in the appropriate direction; use separate directional capacities for full-duplex links. A logical all-to-all implementation may add staging, sorting and protocol overhead above the bound. Changing expert placement changes Vij and can reduce the critical cut without changing the total number of routed assignments. DeepEP, DeepSeek-V3.

Derive the effect of top-k and node coalescing. For T tokens of hidden width h and value size s, independently sending every top-k assignment costs Tkh s payload bytes. Suppose experts are uniformly and independently selected across n nodes, allowing repeated node destinations for this approximation. The probability a particular node receives no assignment for one token is (1−1/n)^k. By summing indicator variables, the expected number of distinct destination nodes is n[1−(1−1/n)^k]. Sending one token copy per destination node before local fanout therefore costs approximately Ths times that distinct-node count, not Tkh s across the slow boundary. Actual routers and without-replacement expert selection can change the distribution.

Example. If n=4 and k=8, the expected distinct-node count is 4[1−(3/4)^8]≈3.600, less than eight independent copies. This is a possible network saving; local fanout and return aggregation still exist. Meanwhile, if one receiving node gets 40 GB and has only 100 GB/s ingress, dispatch cannot finish in less than 0.4 s even if every other link is idle. Mean bytes per rank would hide the bottleneck.

Distributed serving: iteration scheduling to phase separation

Orca and Sarathi-Serve

Orca schedules at generation-iteration granularity so completed requests leave and new ones enter without waiting for an entire static batch. Selective batching handles operations whose request shapes differ. This is a landmark in continuous serving. [16]

Sarathi-Serve chunks prompt processing and mixes bounded prefill work with ongoing decodes. A controlled token budget avoids a huge prompt blocking many next-token steps. Similar-sized iterations also reduce imbalance in a serving pipeline. Smaller chunks can hurt prompt efficiency, so chunk size is chosen against the latency target. [17]

Orca changes the scheduling unit; Sarathi controls its size

A static batch remains tied to its longest output sequence: completed requests leave unused slots while other requests keep decoding. Iteration-level scheduling admits and retires requests between model iterations, so each iteration sees a new active set. That requires persistent per-request KV state and mapping logic; the batch is now a transient compute arrangement rather than the unit of request ownership. Orca made this distinction central to LLM serving. [16]

Not every operation is equally batchable. Linear layers can concatenate tokens across requests into a GEMM. Attention must retain each request's correct context boundaries and causal history. Selective batching avoids pretending that different request lengths form one dense attention sequence. A modern paged/ragged attention kernel supplies another implementation of that same requirement: keep semantic sequence boundaries while changing physical storage and compute grouping.

The original schedule compares two existing decodes A/B with arriving prompts C/D. Prefill-first admission creates long gaps between decode iterations; decode-first admission delays prompt completion. Sarathi-Serve subdivides prompt work and admits it within a token budget together with decode tokens. This regularizes iteration duration and can improve pipeline balance as well as token latency. [17]

The mechanism is more precise than “batch prefill and decode.” Dense layers often have spare arithmetic capacity while loading weights for a small decode batch. Additional prompt tokens can use that capacity up to the point where the GEMM becomes compute limited. Beyond that point, more prompt tokens extend the iteration and hurt token latency. The useful budget depends on model size, TP degree, precision and hardware; it cannot be one universal constant.

Chunking also has costs. Each later prompt chunk attends to the preceding history and may require additional cache reads and kernel launches. Small chunks can reduce GEMM efficiency and lengthen TTFT. A serving scheduler therefore chooses a point on a latency/throughput tradeoff rather than removing the tradeoff entirely. Workloads with long prompts and strict decode deadlines may still favor separate phase pools.

Splitwise and DistServe

Splitwise separates prompt computation and token generation onto hardware suited to each phase, optimizing cost, throughput, or power. DistServe jointly selects phase resources, parallelism, and placement to maximize goodput under TTFT and output-token latency constraints. Their common insight is that phase interference and resource requirements can justify separate pools. [18] [19]

MKV=2LnpromptHKVdhs(equal-width K/V)Ttransfer≥MKVβnetwork,effectiveSeparate if: ΔTinterference+ΔTspecialization>Ttransfer+Textra queue+Trepartition+Tcontrol\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{KV}}&=2L n_{\mathrm{prompt}}H_{\mathrm{KV}}d_h s\quad\text{(equal-width K/V)}\\T_{\mathrm{transfer}}&\ge\frac{M_{\mathrm{KV}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{network,effective}}}\\\text{Separate if: }&\Delta T_{\mathrm{interference}}+\Delta T_{\mathrm{specialization}}\\&>T_{\mathrm{transfer}}+T_{\mathrm{extra\ queue}}+T_{\mathrm{repartition}}+T_{\mathrm{control}}\end{aligned}MKV​Ttransfer​Separate if: ​=2Lnprompt​HKV​dh​s(equal-width K/V)≥βnetwork,effective​MKV​​ΔTinterference​+ΔTspecialization​>Ttransfer​+Textra queue​+Trepartition​+Tcontrol​​

For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, dimension 128, BF16, and 8,192 prompt tokens, M=1 GiB. At 25 GB/s effective bandwidth, the serialization lower bound is about 43 ms. A 131,072-token prompt produces 16 GiB under the same architecture, requiring about 687 ms. Layerwise overlap may hide part of this, but shared traffic can extend it.

The destination may use a different TP degree. KV must then be repartitioned, not merely copied as an opaque byte buffer. Admission must reserve enough destination capacity; otherwise prefill workers produce state that waits in a congested transfer queue.

DistServe: the scheduling objective is goodput, not just utilization

The source plots hold a model fixed and add one prompt to a decode batch. The widening gap for a longer prompt demonstrates why a throughput-friendly mixed batch can violate output-token latency. The resource problem has two parts: interference while work shares a GPU, and coupling of hardware/parallelism choices across phases. Disaggregation addresses both by giving prefill and decode separate queues and execution pools. [19]

This does not imply that disaggregation always beats chunking. It adds weight replicas, KV transfer, destination admission and another queue. At low traffic, a separated pool may sit idle while the other is busy; at long context, KV serialization can consume much of the first-token budget. Splitwise emphasizes hardware specialization and cluster provisioning, whereas DistServe explicitly searches resource and parallelism choices for per-GPU goodput under latency objectives. Their studies answer related but distinct optimization problems. [18]

Queueing can reverse a parallelism choice

Suppose service time for a prompt is D and arrivals are Poisson at rate λ. In the idealized M/D/1 queue, mean waiting time is λD²/[2(1−λD)], defined only for λD<1. Near saturation, waiting grows rapidly. A TP group that reduces isolated service time may use more devices per request; separate replicas may offer more aggregate capacity and lower queueing at higher load. Thus the best configuration for one prompt can differ from the best fleet configuration.

TTFT=Trouting+Tprefill queue+Tprefill+Texposed KV+Tdecode queue+Tfirst decode/controlTPOT=Tdecode+Tscheduling gapsGoodput=completed requests meeting all defined SLOselapsed time\begin{aligned}\mathrm{TTFT}&=T_{\mathrm{routing}}+T_{\mathrm{prefill\ queue}}+T_{\mathrm{prefill}}\\&\quad+T_{\mathrm{exposed\ KV}}+T_{\mathrm{decode\ queue}}+T_{\mathrm{first\ decode/control}}\\\mathrm{TPOT}&=T_{\mathrm{decode}}+T_{\mathrm{scheduling\ gaps}}\\\mathrm{Goodput}&=\frac{\text{completed requests meeting all defined SLOs}}{\text{elapsed time}}\end{aligned}TTFTTPOTGoodput​=Trouting​+Tprefill queue​+Tprefill​+Texposed KV​+Tdecode queue​+Tfirst decode/control​=Tdecode​+Tscheduling gaps​=elapsed timecompleted requests meeting all defined SLOs​​

The mean formula is a teaching model, not a tail-latency guarantee. Real prompts have variable lengths, arrivals burst, outputs have variable lifetimes and batching changes service time dynamically. Those features often make tails worse than a uniform model predicts. DistServe uses profiling and workload-aware planning rather than inferring its entire policy from one isolated kernel measurement.

The top row sweeps offered load. Read the rate at a chosen attainment target, such as the study's 90% requirement, rather than the farthest visible point. The bottom row changes SLO stringency, showing that system capacity depends on the target. A statement such as “7.4× higher rate” is a maximum in a particular setting; it does not mean every model receives that gain, or that throughput and stricter-SLO maxima occur together.

Derivation: why mean service speed and latency under load lead to different placements

Teaching queue. Assume Poisson request arrivals with rate λ, one FCFS server, and independent service durations S with finite first and second moments. Let ρ=λE[S]<1. This M/G/1 model abstracts a fixed request-serving configuration; continuous batching and state-dependent decode speeds do not obey it exactly. The derivation explains the queueing effect relevant to DistServe, rather than reproducing its planner.

1. Compute residual service work seen by an arrival. A service interval of length s contributes area s²/2 under its remaining-work triangle. Over time, λ completed jobs per unit time produce mean residual work R=λE[S²]/2. Longer service intervals are more likely to be encountered, which is why the second moment appears.

2. Add the jobs already waiting. By Little's law, the mean number in the waiting queue is Lq=λWq. Their mean total service work is LqE[S]. Thus an arriving job's mean wait satisfies:

Wq=R+λWqE[S](1−ρ)Wq=λE[S2]2Wq=λE[S2]2(1−ρ)\begin{aligned}W_q&=R+\lambda W_q\mathbb E[S]\\(1-\rho)W_q&=\frac{\lambda\mathbb E[S^2]}2\\W_q&=\frac{\lambda\mathbb E[S^2]}{2(1-\rho)}\end{aligned}Wq​(1−ρ)Wq​Wq​​=R+λWq​E[S]=2λE[S2]​=2(1−ρ)λE[S2]​​

With mean μS and squared coefficient of variation cv²=Var(S)/μS², E[S²]=μS²(1+cv²). At the same mean load, more variable prompts increase waiting. Deterministic service gives cv²=0 and Wq=λμS²/[2(1−ρ)]; exponential service gives cv²=1 and twice that mean wait. Neither determines a p99 SLO by itself.

Example and placement consequence. At λ=8/s and mean service 0.1 s, ρ=0.8. Deterministic jobs have Wq=0.2 s; exponential jobs have Wq=0.4 s. A 100 ms isolated request can therefore have much larger arrival-to-service latency. If using more TP ranks lowers one request's service time but removes independent replicas, compare total capacity and routing among queues as well as isolated latency. Two replicated queues cannot be evaluated by inserting their combined arrival rate into a single-server formula.

Show worked solution
