The same mean service and utilization give very different waiting times because long jobs occupy the server disproportionately. This is a mean-latency model, not a percentile guarantee; admission for a tail SLO requires a service distribution or direct workload measurements.

KV transfer has a layout contract

A prefill worker must transfer the representation the decode worker expects: layer indexing, dtype/scales, token/page order, head partition and model/adapter version. If TP degrees differ, transfer is a redistribution. If KV is quantized differently, conversion may be required and must preserve the intended quality contract. Prefix sharing also needs identity checks so a cache from one model or adapter is not reused under another.

Layerwise streaming can overlap transfer with later prefill layers, but the source must retain each layer's KV until the transfer is complete and the destination must reserve space. RDMA moves bytes efficiently; it does not provide eviction, admission or coherence policy. A robust design accounts for cancellation, transfer failure and partially installed state. Duplicate transfer or delayed acknowledgments should not cause an active request's cache to be reclaimed.

Migration and reuse move the placement decision after arrival

Llumnix makes request placement dynamic: an active request can migrate to relieve a hotspot or satisfy priority. Moving a growing KV cache has a cost, and during copy the request may keep generating more state. Incremental migration must track the delta and finish with a consistent handoff. Mooncake instead places shared KV reuse at the center of a disaggregated service, exploiting CPU/storage capacity and network transfer to avoid recomputation. [20] [21]

Cache-local routing and load balancing can disagree. The worker with a useful prefix may have the longest queue. A useful cost model compares expected recomputation or transfer saved with extra waiting, rather than routing every matching prefix to the same machine. This is one reason serving distribution is fundamentally a stateful scheduling problem, not only model partitioning.

Llumnix and Mooncake

Llumnix migrates active requests and their state to rebalance load, respect priorities, and reduce fragmentation. Migration changes request placement after arrival, at the cost of moving state. Mooncake organizes distributed serving around a shared KV cache and coordinated prefill/decode resources, allowing computation reuse across workers. Cache locality and load balance can conflict: sending every related request to one worker creates a hotspot. [20] [21]

Low-communication and heterogeneous execution

PowerSGD approximates matrix-shaped gradients using low-rank factors and carries compression residuals forward. It reduces transferred bytes but adds local work and approximation. It helps when saved network time exceeds factorization and synchronization overhead while preserving convergence. [23]

DiLoCo performs multiple local optimization steps within device islands before exchanging outer updates. This reduces inter-island synchronization frequency, changing the optimization process. Streaming DiLoCo divides synchronization into parts and overlaps them with computation. Decoupled DiLoCo extends the family toward asynchronous, failure-resilient progress. These methods move a system boundary: fast synchronized work remains within an island, while coordination between islands becomes less frequent or less tightly coupled. [24] [25] [26]

Petals instead distributes transformer blocks across heterogeneous participants for inference and efficient finetuning. Its tradeoff is access to aggregate capacity versus network latency, worker churn, and trust in remote execution. It is a different objective from minimizing latency on a private tightly connected accelerator cluster. [27]

Alpa automates choices among operator and pipeline partitions with cost modeling and search. Automation reduces manual search but inherits the cost model’s assumptions. Dynamic request lengths, MoE routing, and network contention make fixed training profiles less predictive for serving. [15]

DiLoCo: change synchronization frequency, not merely packet size

A synchronous data-parallel step evaluates gradients at the same parameter point, averages them and applies an update. DiLoCo allows each island to perform H local optimizer steps before global coordination. At outer step t, replica i starts from θt and reaches θt,i after local training. The averaged displacement is treated as an outer gradient, and an outer optimizer updates the shared model. The paper uses AdamW internally and Nesterov momentum externally. [24]

Initialize each island: θt,i,0 = θt
For h=0,…,H−1:
    θt,i,h+1 = InnerOpt(θt,i,h, local_gradient)
Δt = (1/K) Σi (θt − θt,i,H)
θt+1 = OuterOpt(θt, Δt)

This is not identical to accumulating H minibatch gradients at a fixed θt. Local parameters change between steps, and optimizer state introduces path dependence. It is also not ordinary parameter averaging unless the outer optimizer has that special form. The communication saving comes with a changed optimization trajectory that must be evaluated for convergence and data heterogeneity.

An island may itself contain tightly connected TP/PP/FSDP ranks; DiLoCo only relaxes the boundary between islands. Every island still needs enough capacity to train a full replica through its internal partition. Reducing inter-island communication does not make an individual model shard independently trainable without its ordinary per-layer dependencies.

Derivation: local steps save communication by changing the optimization trajectory

Simplified local-SGD model. This derivation isolates why infrequent synchronization differs from synchronous data parallelism. Two workers start at θ₀ and take H plain gradient steps on local objectives fi with the same learning rate η, then average parameters. The actual DiLoCo recipe uses an inner optimizer and an outer momentum optimizer, so the calculation is explanatory rather than its complete update rule.

1. Expand two local steps. Let gi=∇fi(θ₀) and Hi=∇²fi(θ₀). For small η and smooth fi:

θi,1=θ0−ηgi∇fi(θi,1)≈gi−ηHigiθi,2≈θ0−2ηgi+η2Higiθˉ2≈θ0−2ηgˉ+η2mean⁡i(Higi)\begin{aligned}\theta_{i,1}&=\theta_0-\eta g_i\\\nabla f_i(\theta_{i,1})&\approx g_i-\eta H_i g_i\\\theta_{i,2}&\approx\theta_0-2\eta g_i+\eta^2H_i g_i\\\bar\theta_2&\approx\theta_0-2\eta\bar g+\eta^2\operatorname{mean}_i(H_i g_i)\end{aligned}θi,1​∇fi​(θi,1​)θi,2​θˉ2​​=θ0​−ηgi​≈gi​−ηHi​gi​≈θ0​−2ηgi​+η2Hi​gi​≈θ0​−2ηgˉ​+η2meani​(Hi​gi​)​

By contrast, two synchronous steps on the mean objective give θsync,2≈θ₀−2ηḡ+η²H̄ḡ. The difference is η²[average(Hi gi)−H̄ḡ], a curvature/gradient heterogeneity term. It vanishes in special cases, but generally does not. Reducing synchronization is therefore an algorithmic change, not simply sending identical gradients less often.

2. Verify with an exact scalar example. Take f₁(θ)=θ²/2 and f₂(θ)=3(θ−2)²/2, θ₀=0 and η=0.1. Worker 1 stays at zero; worker 2 moves to 0.6, then 1.02. Their mean is 0.51. The mean objective has gradient 2θ−3, so synchronous steps move 0→0.3→0.54. The 0.03 difference is already present after two steps without stochastic noise.

3. Relate the saved network to the changed update. If one global exchange costs tnet and H local steps each cost tstep, a no-overlap cycle costs Htstep+tnet; communication fraction is tnet/(Htstep+tnet). Raising H reduces that fraction but increases opportunities for local trajectories to diverge. A real comparison must measure quality at matched data/compute and wall time, including the outer optimizer, rather than claiming the same update with fewer packets. Streaming synchronization additionally introduces delay, which creates another departure from the synchronous trajectory.

Streaming DiLoCo: lower peaks and tolerate delay

Full-model synchronization every H steps creates a burst. Streaming DiLoCo partitions parameters into fragments and synchronizes different fragments at different times. The figure's colors identify these fragments; the model is temporarily a combination of components last synchronized at different moments. Fragment size and order control peak traffic and the overlap opportunity, while delayed synchronization and blending affect optimization. [25]

The schedule compares full bursts, fragmented exchange and communication overlapped with later work. Purple communication can move off the critical path if it finishes before the fragment is needed under the algorithm's delay policy. The plot is simulated from step and network assumptions; the paper separately reports model training experiments. Its large-model utilization estimates should not be described as measured training runs on those model sizes.

The reported empirical range includes models from tens of millions to 4B parameters and an overtraining study on a 1B model. Evidence that delayed/low-bit outer updates work there is valuable but does not prove arbitrary staleness is harmless at frontier scale. The later Decoupled DiLoCo line further investigates progress and failure decoupling; evaluate each variant's accepted delay, worker participation and optimizer semantics rather than treating the family name as one protocol. [26]

Compression, local steps and asynchronous progress are separate axes

PowerSGD reduces the representation of each synchronized matrix gradient using low-rank factors and residual error feedback. DiLoCo reduces synchronization frequency. Streaming schedules reduce burstiness and overlap transfers. Asynchronous variants relax when workers must agree. These axes can compose, but their numerical effects accumulate. A fair comparison fixes total compute/tokens, target loss and wall time, and includes compression/outer-optimizer overhead. [23]

For a matrix gradient G∈R^(m×n), rank-r factors need roughly r(m+n) values rather than mn. That saving is useful only when r is small enough and factorization plus extra reductions cost less than the traffic avoided. Error feedback retains the unsent residual so discarded information can influence future updates. It reduces systematic compression loss but is not a universal proof of unchanged training for every optimizer and schedule.

Heterogeneous collaborative inference such as Petals pursues a different objective: access a model across available machines even when no participant owns a full accelerator cluster. The autoregressive path crosses remotely hosted depth blocks, so latency accumulates across network boundaries and worker churn matters. It should be compared with available alternatives at the same resource/access constraint, not ranked against a tightly coupled private cluster as if the deployment goal were identical. [27]

The practical comparison should fix model quality, traffic, hardware budget, and SLO. Re-run current baselines: newer engines may already include techniques proposed in older papers. Paper speedups are evidence that a mechanism mattered in a particular experiment, not permanent multipliers.

Diagnose a slow cluster systematically

SymptomLikely causesUseful evidence
More TP ranks increase token latencyCollective startup, narrow GEMMs, cross-node placementPer-layer compute/communication trace
GPUs idle togetherData input stalls, global barriers, checkpoint pauseCPU, storage, and collective timelines
One rank consistently finishes lateUneven layer cost, hot experts, slow linkPer-rank time and routed-token counts
FSDP/ZeRO-3 fits but is slowRepeated parameter gathering, poor prefetch, too-small unitsAll-gather bytes and overlap windows
Long-context throughput collapsesAttention work, KV traffic, causal imbalanceContext-length sweep and shard timing
Low mean latency but poor p99Queueing, migrations, bursts, long-prefill interferenceRequest-level traces at realistic arrival rates
Network benchmark looks fast, application slowDifferent message size, concurrency, topology, CPU launch overheadIn-application collective distributions

Maintain consistent collective order across ranks. A conditional branch that makes one rank skip a collective can deadlock the group. Check tensor shapes and process-group membership before blaming the network. For reproducibility, record group dimensions and their mapping to physical nodes.

Worked mapping: 64 ranks are a mesh, not a bag of GPUs

Consider eight nodes with eight tightly connected accelerators each. One possible dense-training factorization is TP=8, PP=2, DP=4. Each TP group fits within a node; two nodes form a pipeline replica; four pipeline replicas process different data. A rank can be indexed by (data_rank, pipeline_rank, tensor_rank). Different collectives vary different coordinates while holding the others fixed. This defines who actually participates, avoiding the common mistake of launching a reduction across every rank for every tensor.

If ZeRO is applied across the data coordinate, each TP/PP shard's optimizer state is distributed among four owners. It is not divided by 64 again after already accounting for TP/PP parameter ownership. If context parallelism is added, either some existing dimension must shrink or more devices are required; EP may share or replace a data dimension depending on the framework. The product of independent mesh dimensions equals the rank count, but not every feature named “parallelism” is an independent multiplicative axis.

Compare two candidate changes with the critical path

Suppose a profiled iteration spends 100 ms in compute, 25 ms in exposed TP communication and 10 ms in an exposed gradient tail. Halving the gradient payload can save at most 5 ms under a bandwidth-only assumption, even though gradient bytes may dominate total traffic. Eliminating half the exposed TP time could save 12.5 ms. Conversely, if a TP collective is already fully overlapped, reducing its isolated duration may save nothing. These are derived bounds from a hypothetical trace, illustrating why bytes alone cannot prioritize work.

Now suppose a memory optimization allows twice the microbatch size. That may improve matrix utilization and reduce pipeline bubbles per useful token, even if it adds one parameter gather. The correct comparison reprofiles the new schedule and global batch semantics; it cannot add a memory percentage and subtract a communication percentage as independent factors.

Validate semantics before benchmarking

For a small deterministic model, compare the distributed forward output and parameter gradients with a single-device reference within the expected rounding tolerance. Test variable sequence lengths, masked/padded tokens, tied embeddings and uneven last microbatches. Verify that loss normalization uses the total count of valid tokens, rather than averaging per-rank means when token counts differ. Check global clipping and optimizer statistics over unique parameter elements.

For inference, compare logits or the intended sampling distribution, not only decoded strings from one seed. A sharded top-k shortcut can silently drop a globally relevant token. For context parallelism, verify causal masks and positional indices after layout permutation. For MoE, verify dispatch/combine ordering and weighting when multiple routes share a destination. For KV migration, verify request/model identity and state consistency after handoff.

Only then run scale and load sweeps. Record per-rank durations, memory high-water marks and communication distributions so a regression can be attributed to a particular dependency or resource. A professional distributed result is a correct computation plus an explained performance change.

A design recipe and the main insights

Start with the smallest partition that fits and meets latency. Use serving replicas for independent traffic. Add TP where local bandwidth and compute savings justify per-layer communication. Add PP when depth partitioning improves capacity without intolerable bubbles. Shard optimizer state for training memory, and use context parallelism when sequence state dominates. Add EP for expert placement, with route-aware load measurement.

For a 64-device training cluster, an illustrative mapping is TP=8, PP=2, DP=4. This is a logical factorization, not a recommendation for every model. ZeRO operates over chosen data groups; EP can replace or intersect dimensions depending on the framework. Multiplying every named degree blindly can double-count ranks.

The key insight is communication frequency often matters as much as volume. Training gradients can be amortized across accumulation; TP reductions are on the token’s critical path; cold KV restoration may occur once; expert dispatch repeats at every MoE layer. Designing the cluster means placing each dependency on a link and schedule that can sustain it.

References & reading route

Primary papers and official technical documents. Dates identify first reports or publication, not a claim of independent reproduction. Numerical results retain their original conditions.

  1. NCCL collective operations documentation. All-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, and communication semantics.
  2. Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (2019). Column/row tensor partitioning for transformer layers.
  3. Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (2021). Composition of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism.
  4. GPipe (2018/2019). Microbatch pipeline parallelism with synchronous updates.
  5. PipeDream (2018/2019). Pipeline scheduling and weight-version management.
  6. Memory-Efficient Pipeline-Parallel DNN Training (2020/2021). PipeDream-2BW, bounded weight buffering.
  7. ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (2019/2020). Shard optimizer, gradients, and parameters in successive stages.
  8. ZeRO-Infinity (2021). GPU, CPU, and NVMe offload with scheduling and prefetch.
  9. Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models (2022). Sequence parallelism and selective recomputation.
  10. DeepSpeed Ulysses (2023). Sequence-to-head redistribution through all-to-all.
  11. Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context (2023). Stream attention blocks around a device ring.
  12. USP: A Unified Sequence Parallelism Approach (2024). Combine all-to-all and ring strategies to match topology.
  13. Zero Bubble Pipeline Parallelism (2023/2024). Separate input-gradient and weight-gradient work for better scheduling.
  14. DualPipe and DualPipeV official repository (2025 onward). Bidirectional scheduling and computation/communication overlap; implementation constraints.
  15. Alpa: Automating Inter- and Intra-Operator Parallelism (2022). Search over stage and operator partitioning with cost models.
  16. Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (2022). Iteration-level scheduling and selective batching.
  17. Sarathi-Serve (2024). Chunked prefills and stall-free batching.
  18. Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting (2023/2024). Hardware-aware separation of prompt processing and generation.
  19. DistServe (2024). Disaggregate phases and optimize per-GPU goodput under SLOs.
  20. Llumnix: Dynamic Scheduling for LLM Serving (2024). Live request/KV migration for load balancing and priorities.
  21. Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture (2024). Shared cache and distributed prefill/decode serving.
  22. DeepEP official repository. Expert-parallel communication; version-sensitive library.
  23. PowerSGD: Practical Low-Rank Gradient Compression (2019). Low-rank factors and error feedback reduce gradient communication.
  24. DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training (2023/2024). Local optimization and infrequent outer synchronization.
  25. Streaming DiLoCo with Overlapping Communication (2025). Fragmented synchronization overlapped with computation.
  26. Decoupled DiLoCo for Resilient Distributed Pre-training (2026). Decouple asynchronous system progress from tight global synchronization.
  27. Petals: Collaborative Inference and Fine-tuning of Large Models (2022/2023). Distributed blocks over heterogeneous participating machines.
  28. PyTorch FSDP: Experiences on Scaling Fully Sharded Data Parallel (2023). Parameter lifetime, prefetch, rate limiting, and implementation constraints.
  29. Getting Started with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2). Per-parameter DTensor representation, fully_shard and implicit/explicit prefetch.
  30. PyTorch FullyShardedDataParallel documentation. Sharding strategies, backward prefetch, resharding, and optimizer parameter caveats.
  31. Mesh-TensorFlow: Deep Learning for Supercomputers (2018). Named tensor dimensions mapped to device-mesh dimensions.
  32. GSPMD: General and Scalable Parallelization for ML Computation Graphs (2021). Compiler sharding propagation and collective insertion.
  33. FLUX: Fast Software-based Communication Overlap On GPUs Through Kernel Fusion (2024). Fine-grained overlap of tensor-parallel communication with dependent GEMM tiles.
